MINUTES
  Regular Meeting
  ALHAMBRA CITY COUNCIL
  April 13, 2026
  6:00 p.m.

ROLL CALL: At 6:10 p.m., on Monday, April 13, 2026, the Alhambra City Council met in the Council
Chambers of Alhambra City Hall.

PRESENT:  LEE, MAZA, WANG, ANDRADE-STADLER, MALONEY
ABSENT:  NONE

Officials Present: City Manager Binnquist, Assistant City Manager Garcia, City Attorney Montes,
Assistant City Clerk Lamb McCarthy, Director of Parks and Recreation Macias, Director of Finance
Lieu, Director of Community Development Ho, Planning Manager McCurley, Director of Public Works
and Utilities Ahlen, Chief of Fire Department Ragusa, Battalion Chief Brown, Chief of Police Kennedy,
Assistant Police Chief Fuentes, Director of Library Services LohGuan, Director of Human Resources
Ko, Management Analyst Alvarez

FLAG SALUTE:  Led by Mayor Maloney

LAND ACKNOWLEDGEMENT: We acknowledge that the land on which we are gathered is the
traditional, ancestral, and unceded territory of the Gabrielino/Tongva peoples. We seek to prioritize
respect for the historic culture and contemporary presence of the native peoples throughout California,
especially in the greater Los Angeles/Alhambra area. We come with respect and gratitude for the
Gabrielino/Tongva people who still consider themselves the caretakers of this land. It is through their
examples that we are reminded of our greater responsibility to take care of Mother Earth and to take
care of each other.

CEREMONIALS

PUBLIC HEARINGS

2.  EDWARD BYRNE MEMORIAL JUSTICE ASSISTANCE GRANT (JAG) – F2M5-41,
  N2M26-36, M2M26-57

  2
4-13-26
   This was the time and place set by Notice No. N2M26-36 for the City Council to hold a
  public hearing to receive community input concerning the use of funds received under the
  United States Department of Justice, Bureau of Justice Assistance Edward Byrne
  Memorial Justice Assistance Grant (JAG) Program. Assistant Police Chief FUENTES
  delivered a staff report. The City of Alhambra was eligible to receive $12,714.00. The
  formula used to determine the amount each jurisdiction is eligible for is based upon a
  minimum base allocation, population, and major crime statistics. The 2025 JAG funds
  would be used for personal protective equipment for police officers during high-risk
  incidents. The grant guidelines require the City conduct a public hearing to receive
  community input concerning the use of funds, and approval of the application and pertinent
  requirements. Once the City Council designate the Police Chief as the JAG Grant
  Administrator, the Police Chief or his Designee would be responsible for the expenditure
  of funds, monitoring the award, and submitting the required reports.

  Opened & Closed the Public Hearing: Mayor MALONEY opened the public hearing and as
  there was no one present who wished to speak, closed the same.

  Discussion:  Vice Mayor ANDRADE-STADLER and Assistant Chief FUENTES
  discussed the annual funding source.

  Action Taken:  After receiving public testimony, the Mayor closed the public
  hearing and the Council adopted Minute Order No. M2M26-57 as follows:

  RESOLVED by the Alhambra City Council that this Council hereby authorizes
  the City Manager, or her designee, to apply for United States Department of
  Justice, Bureau of Justice Assistance -- Edward Byrne Memorial Justice
  Assistance Grant (JAG) Program funds in the amount of $12,714.00 and
  appropriates expenditure and revenue funds in the amount of $12,714.00 in
  FY 2025-26 upon grant award; and,

  BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED by the Alhambra City Council that this Council
  hereby ratifies the action of the City Manager in designating the Chief of Police
  or Designee as the administrator for said Grant and directs staff to undertake
  the steps necessary to finalize Council’s action.

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded:  MAZA
  Ayes:  MAZA, WANG, ANDRADE-STADLER, LEE, MALONEY
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

3.  PUBLIC HEARING TO ADOPT ORDINANCE NO. O2M26-4860 APPROVING ZONING
  TEXT AMENDMENT AMD-26-03, AMENDING THE ALHAMBRA MUNICIPAL CODE TO
  UPDATE CHAPTER 23.15 (INCLUSIONARY HOUSING); ADOPT RESOLUTION NO.
  R2M26-8 UPDATING THE INCLUSIONARY HOUSING REGULATIONS AND
  INCLUSIONARY HOUSING IN-LIEU FEE SCHEDULE; AND DETERMINE THIS
  ACTION IS EXEMPT FROM CEQA – F2M18-35, N2M26-34, R2M26-8, O2M26-4860

  This was the time and place set by Notice No. N2M26-34 for the City Council to hold a
  public hearing to consider an ordinance approving a Zoning Text Amendment to amend
  Title 23 (Zoning) of the Alhambra Municipal Code to update Chapter 23.15 (Inclusionary
  Housing) consistent with the objectives of the City’s adopted 2021-2029 Housing Element.
  Community Development Director HO delivered a staff report. Paul PENINGER, from BAE
  3
4-13-26
   Urban Economics working with Environmental Science Associates (ESA), delivered a
  PowerPoint presentation, which is on file in the City Clerk’s office. Zoning Text
  Amendment AMD-26-03 was a City-initiated update to the City’s Inclusionary Housing
  Ordinance (IHO). Based on the proposed updates to the IHO, updates were also required
  to the Inclusionary Housing Regulations and Inclusionary Housing In-Lieu Fee schedule.
  The proposed updates were informed by implementation of the IHO over the past five (5)
  years and were intended to improve clarity as well as align with state housing law-
  specifically, State Density Bonus Law. The proposed amendments maintained the City’s
  15% inclusionary unit requirement while revising affordability level requirements and
  simplifying compliance mechanisms. Updates to the Inclusionary Housing Regulations
  and Inclusionary Housing In-Lieu Fee schedule would ensure consistency with the
  proposed IHO updates. Adoption of these proposed updates aligns with the goals,
  policies, and objectives set forth in the City’s 2021-2029 Housing Element. Any fees
  collected under the proposed updated Inclusionary Housing In-Lieu Fee Schedule would
  be deposited into the City’s Inclusionary Housing Trust Fund pursuant to the provisions of
  the proposed Inclusionary Housing Ordinance and proposed Inclusionary Housing
  Regulations.

  The City reviewed the environmental impacts of this Ordinance under the California
  Environmental Quality Act (Public Resources Code §§ 21000, et seq. “CEQA”) and the
  regulations promulgated thereunder (14 Cal. Code of Regs. §§ 15000, et seq., the “CEQA
  Guidelines”). This Ordinance was not subject to further review environmental review
  because: (1) it would not result in a direct or reasonably foreseeable indirect physical
  change in the environment (14 Cal. Code Regs. § 15060(c)(2)); (2) there was no possibility
  that this Ordinance would have a significant effect on the environment (14 Cal. Code Regs.
  § 15061(b)(3)); and (3) the Ordinance, by itself, did not constitute a “project” as defined in
  section 21065 of the Public Resources Code and the CEQA Guidelines (14 Cal. Code
  Regs. § 15378). It could be seen with certainty that there was no possibility that this
  Ordinance would have a significant effect on the environment.

  City Manager BINNQUIST noted that there were corrections made to the in-lieu fee
  schedule as shown in the PowerPoint presentation and that the updated presentation
  would be available to the public and on file in the City Clerk’s office.

  Open Public Hearing:  Mayor Maloney opened the public hearing.

  Public Comment:
  1) Lewis Mccammon agreed with the recommendations overall and expressed some
  concerns with the practice in allowing in-lieu fees which results in a continued lack of
  constructed affordable units. He also discussed difficulties in providing more for-sale
  units rather than more affordable rental units and referred to the project at 110 S.
  Chapel Ave. which evicted tenants.

  2) Melissa Michelson discussed the in-lieu fee schedule recommendations and noted
  that staff recommendations were too low. She further expressed concerns with the in-
  lieu fees and the lack of constructed affordable units.

  3) Adam Bray-Ali expressed concerns with the in-lieu fees and the lack of constructed
  affordable housing units. He stated that the needed to be less rules and allow for
  simple building permits to encourage construction.

  4
4-13-26
   4) Alborz Motashami, via Zoom, expressed concerns with in-lieu fees and the lack of
  constructed affordable housing units and made several recommendations regarding
  the IHO such as density bonuses, lower construction fees, and lower parking
  minimums.

  5) Simon Gibbons, via Zoom, expressed concerns with the restrictions in the IHO and
  asked Council exercise caution.

  City Attorney MONTES made clarifications regarding the density bonus benefits under the
  current housing ordinances in response to public comment. He further explained the
  recommendations from staff and the Planning Commission.

  Close Public Hearing:  After receiving public comment, Mayor Maloney closed the
  public hearing.

  Discussion:  Vice Mayor ANDRADE-STADLER discussed in-lieu fees not
  included in the development and the relation to the Housing Trust Fund with Mr. MONTES
  and Mr. HO.

  Councilmember WANG further discussed the City’s ability to use the in-lieu fees for the
  Housing Trust Fund, the in-lieu fee calculation regarding for sale units, the in-lieu fee
  schedule comparison with regards to staff recommendations and Planning Commission
  recommendations. Mr. HO provided clarification Ms. WANG and Mr. HO discussed the
  Planning Commission recommendations and staff recommendations as they would help
  the City achieve its RHNA goals.

  Councilmember MAZA supported staff recommendations for the fee schedule overall as
  it would help the City achieve its RHNA goals. He further discussed staff’s reasoning for
  their recommendations with Mr. HO. They also discussed increasing the density bonuses,
  as seen in the Commercial Business District (CBD) with Mr. MONTES and Planning
  Manager MCCURLEY. Mr. MAZA supported staff recommendations.

  Councilmember LEE discussed in-lieu fees schedule in the staff report and the Housing
  Trust Fund with Mr. HO. Ms. LEE expressed that the fees collected were not significantly
  contributing to the Housing Trust Fund and suggested that projects of 5 or fewer units
  would have to pay in-lieu fees and projects of 6 or more units would have to set aside
  affordable units. Ms. LEE and Mr. MONTES further discussed density bonuses in the
  ordinance and in California state law and in-lieu fees. Ms. LEE motioned to increase the
  in-lieu fees per square foot for rental and sale units and to change the threshold for in-lieu
  fees from 20 units to 5 units.

  Mr. MAZA opposed the motion for the ways it would hinder developers and limit the ways
  fees are leveraged for larger projects.

  Mayor MALONEY continued to discuss in-lieu fees and the ways the City could support
  affordable units, balancing State density bonus law, and the housing ordinances for
  neighboring cities. He encouraged staff to review other methods to encourage housing
  development in medium and high-density zones by reducing fees. He went on to discuss
  the in-lieu fee formula and capitalization rate with Mr. PENINGER. Mr. PENNINGER
  provided additional clarification to Council’s comments with input from Mr. MONTES. Mr.
  MALONEY supported staff recommendations.
  5
4-13-26
   Council discussed Ms. LEE’s motion. Ms. WANG recognized Ms. Lee’s concerns and
  noted the challenges of the lack of affordable housing available as well as hindrances to
  developers. She stated that she was open to continued discussion and suggested staff
  continue to explore options to further strengthen the IHO rather than accept staff’s current
  recommendations. After questions from Mr. MALONEY, Ms. WANG clarified that she
  would like staff to explore other options to increase affordability for future discussion.

  Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER suggested this program was part of several Strategic Plan
  goals and supported accepting staff recommendations. She stated that Council could
  review other options at a later date and separate discussion. Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER
  motioned to accept staff recommendations to amend the IHO, which was seconded by Mr.
  MAZA. There was no second for Ms. Lee’s motion and it therefore failed. Mr. MALONEY
  supported continued discussion regarding additional options to increase affordable
  housing in Alhambra. Council continued to discuss Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER’S motion.
  Ms. LEE proposed a substitute motion for staff to bring back options to increase in-lieu
  fees for developments. Having received no second, the motion failed. Council returned to
  Ms. Andrade-Stadler’s motion and voted.

  Action Taken:  City Council:

  1.  Conducted a Public Hearing to receive public testimony;

  2.  Directed staff to accept staff’s recommendations for the amended IHO and directed
  the City Attorney to introduce and give first reading by title only, waiving further
  reading to the following ordinance entitled:

  Ordinance No. O2M26-4860: An Ordinance of the City Council of the City of
  Alhambra, California adopting Zoning Text Amendment AMD-26-03, amending the
  Alhambra Municipal Code to update Chapter 23.15 (Inclusionary Housing)

  which ordinance shall return for a second reading and adoption at the next City
  Council meeting on April 27, 2026;

  3.  Adopted the following Resolution entitled: Resolution No. R2M26-8: A Resolution
  of the City Council of the City of Alhambra, California adopting updated
  Inclusionary Housing Regulations and an updated Inclusionary Housing In-Lieu
  Fee Schedule; and,

  4.  Determined this action is exempt from CEQA.

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded:  MAZA
  Ayes:  WANG, ANDRADE-STADLER, MAZA, MALONEY
  Noes:  NONE
  Abstain:  LEE
  Absent:  NONE

4.  HOUSING ELEMENT IMPLEMENTATION PROGRAM 30 (AFFIRMATIVELY
  FURTHERING FAIR HOUSING): REPORT AND PRESENTATION ON TENANT
  PROTECTION STRATEGIES – F2M20-37

  6
4-13-26
   Community Development Director HO delivered a staff report. The City’s 6th Cycle 2021-
  2029 Housing Element included actions to Affirmatively Further Fair Housing (AFFH).
  Specifically, as part of Housing Element Program 30 (Affirmatively Furthering Fair
  Housing), under the fair housing issue of “disproportionate housing need”, the City
  committed to providing a report to City Council detailing alternatives for mitigating rent
  increases for lower income residents to reduce displacement risk. The City’s Housing
  Element Implementation consultant team, Environmental Science Associates (ESA) and
  Veronica Tam and Associates (VTA), prepared a report in alignment with the actions
  identified in the City’s Housing Element. Strategies outlined in the report would assist the
  City in considering, developing, and implementing rent increase and displacement risk
  mitigation measures consistent with commitments in the Housing Element. The complete
  report was included in the April 13, 2026 staff report by the Director of Community
  Development. ESA and VTA’s report summarized the various tenant protection strategies
  the City may consider, and identified the three broad categories that each strategy falls
  within: (1) Controlling Rent Increases; (2) Protecting against eviction and displacement;
  and (3) Preserving and expanding supply of affordable housing. Ms. Veronica Tam,
  Principal, Veronica TAM and Associates presented information regarding the Housing
  Element Implementation tenant protection strategies. Ms. TAM delivered a PowerPoint
  presentation, which is on file in the City Clerk’s office.

  Public Comment:
  1) Adam Bray Ali spoke against rent control measures.

  2) Brian Otis spoke against rent control measures and provided an article to Council,
  which is on file in the City Clerk’s office.

  3) Kenneth Otis spoke against rent control measures.

  4) Lewis McCammon referred to the project at 110 S. Chapel Ave, the lack of new
  affordable units in the City and expiring rent covenants.

  5) David Bond spoke in favor of rent control measures.

  6) Jesus Rojas, representing AAGLA, requested more information be provided to Council
  and the public. He requested Council conduct town hall meetings to receive additional
  public input.

  7) Shirley Tatsuno spoke in support of “mom and pop” landlords and rising costs of
  improvements and repairs.

  8) Melissa Michelson spoke in favor of tenant protections and requested more
  information to be provided to Council and the public.

  9) Sawyer Brooks requested more information to be provided to Council and the public
  regarding rent control and building.

  10) Alborz Mohtashami spoke in favor of more housing options for renters such as the IHO
  and density bonuses.

  7
4-13-26
   Discussion:  Councilmember LEE highlighted protections against rent evictions
  and relocation assistance, including extending recent rental protections and legislation like
  SB 567, set to expire in January 2030. The council can enact an ordinance to extend these
  measures, especially along Main Street, with Lee showing empathy for displaced tenants

  Councilmember MAZA nothing balancing residents' needs with state support,

  Vice Mayor ANDRADE-STADLER highly encouraged housing rights summit, emphasizing

  Councilmember WANG received clarification that some of the proposed measures are

  Mayor MALONEY spoke in support for eviction protections, improving relocation support,

  Action Taken:  City Council received and filed this report.

RECESS & RECONVENE:  Mayor Maloney called for a brief recess at 9:50 p.m. and

5.  REVIEW OF LOCAL TENANT RELOCATION ASSISTANCE PROGRAMS – F2M26-7

  Management Analyst ALVAREZ delivered a staff report. On February 23, 2026, the City
  Council directed staff to research and provide information regarding tenant relocation
  assistance programs. In 2019, the State of California adopted Assembly Bill 1482 (AB
  1482), the Tenant Protection Act of 2019, which established statewide tenant protections
  including rent stabilization and just cause eviction requirements (i.e., default in payment
  of rent, breach of a material term of lease, maintaining a nuisance, engaging in criminal
  activity, tenant’s refusal to allow the owner to enter the residential property). Under AB
  1482, landlords are required to provide relocation assistance for certain no-fault evictions,
  including owner move-in, substantial rehabilitation, demolition, or withdrawal of units from
  the rental market. The required relocation assistance is equal to one month of the tenant’s
  rent or a waiver of the final month’s rent. Payment must be provided within 15 calendar
  days of the notice of termination. AB 1482 establishes a minimum statewide standard;
  however, it does not preclude local jurisdictions from adopting more protective tenant
  regulations, including higher relocation assistance amounts or expanded tenant
  protections. Staff reviewed tenant relocation assistance programs across multiple
  jurisdictions and will present a review of those programs as well as policy options for
  consideration to the City Council.

  Public Comment:
  The following people spoke in favor of tenant relocation assistance:

  2) Alborz Mohtashami
  3) Lewis McCammon, who also provided a handout to Council which is on file in
  the City Clerk’s office.
  4) Melissa Michelson
  5) Sawyer Brooks

  The following people spoke against tenant relocation assistance:
  1) Adam Bray-Ali
  2) Jesus Rojas

  Discussion:  Vice Mayor ANDRADE-STADLER supported Option 2 and
  discussed the tiered structure Option 3 with Mr. ALVAREZ, who provided clarification.

  Councilmember WANG spoke regarding the difficulties of property ownership but stressed
  the need to keep people housed. She supported Option 2 to strengthen tenant relocation

  Councilmember MAZA supported Option 2 and spoke to the ability to keep the process
  simple for the City to enact. He referred to public comment and discussed the difficulty in
  monitoring the variety of needs for each tenant, supported an equal approach of offering
  three months assistance, and supported the property owner paying the assistance rather
  than the City. He further discussed Option 2 with Mr. ALVAREZ, who provided clarification.

  Councilmember LEE supported tenant relocation assistance and discussed the project at
  110 S. Chapel Ave, housing as a right, and the need for regulation over housing. She
  further discussed Option 2 with Mr. ALVAREZ, who provided clarification regarding
  implementation and its use in Burbank. City Manager BINNQUIST provided clarification
  regarding monitoring the program. Ms. LEE motioned to approve an ordinance.

  Mayor MALONEY and Ms. BINNQUIST discussed the definition of “no fault eviction” and
  the cases in which the ordinance would apply. Mr. ALVAREZ and Ms. BINNQUIST stated
  that staff could provide more information as to the different cases of eviction. Mr.
  MALONEY went on to discuss housing as a right, the intricacies of housing choices, and
  the need to increase the number of affordable units in Alhambra. He supported Option 2
  to provide 3 months of tenant relocation assistance. He seconded Ms. Lee’s motion. He
  noted that he would like more information regarding evictions and existing State law, and
  Ms. BINNQUIST provided clarification.

  Action Taken:  City Council directed staff to bring back an ordinance for Option 2
  which would provide relocation assistance of 3 months of rent for no-fault evictions.

6.  MID-CYCLE REPORT AND PRESENTATION ON THE CITY OF ALHAMBRA 6TH
  CYCLE (2021-2029) HOUSING ELEMENT – F2M20-37

  Director of Community Development HO delivered a staff report. Alison LENCI and
  9
4-13-26
   Shannon WAGES, of Environmental Science Associates (ESA) delivered a PowerPoint
  Presentation, which is on file in the City Clerk’s office. The State of California Department
  of Housing and Community Development (HCD) mandates that all jurisdictions report on
  the progress of Housing Element program implementation annually, through Housing
  Element Annual Progress Reports (APR), and through a mid-cycle report half-way through
  the 2021-2029 planning period. This report described the City’s approach and
  methodology to managing implementation of the City’s 6th Cycle HE and summarized the
  status of all 40 programs as of April 2026. The City and Environmental Science Associates
  (ESA), the City’s selected consultant for the oversight and management of Implementation
  Programs contained in the 2021-2029 6th Cycle Housing Element, began working together
  on implementation of HE Programs in October 2024 and have continued to work
  collaboratively to meet the quantified objectives outlined in the City’s HE. The City and
  ESA team’s methodology and approach toward implementation; status of program
  implementation; community engagement and outreach efforts; and tracking, monitoring,
  and reporting progress are summarized in the April 13, 2026 staff report by the Director of
  Community Development.

  Public Comment:
  1) Alborz Mohtashami made additional suggestions to enhance the HE and expand its
  scope.

  2) David Bond suggested public housing options with more partnerships with public and
  private organizations.

  3) Lewis McCammon supported the report and requested additional analysis regarding
  RHNA Cycle 6 Goals.

  4) Shirley Tatsuno supported more affordable housing projects.

  5) Adam Bray-Ali asked for clarification regarding Emergency Ordinance restrictions on
  SB9 and noted that it could allow for more housing to be built.

  Discussion:  Vice Mayor ANDRADE-STADLER thanked the public for their input
  and staff for their work. Councilmember WANG thanked staff for their work on the
  presentation and went on to discuss the RHNA Cycle and the Housing Element. She
  requested more emphasis to increase housing units and conduct public outreach to gain
  input and educate the public. She suggested the City create a task force to address
  Housing issues. Councilmember MAZA supported Ms. Wang’s comments.
  Councilmember LEE also discussed the City’s RHNA goals and previous attempts to
  request a reduction in the allocation goals. She also discussed SB9 and the fallacies in
  “supply and demand” theory when applied to housing. Mayor MALONEY and Mr. HO
  discussed changing the priorities on the Housing Element and accomplishing goals. Mr.
  MALONEY went on to discuss housing issues in California, the lack of available affordable
  housing, and the need to produce more housing options.

  Action Taken:  City Council received and filed this report.

 7.  ACCEPT A DONATION OF A SCOREBOARD FROM EAST ALHAMBRA LITTLE
  LEAGUE AND APPROPRIATION OF FUNDS FOR INSTALLATION – F2M26-12,
  M2M26-58

  East Alhambra Little League purchased a scoreboard and remote control. East Alhambra
  Little League wanted to donate the scoreboard to the City of Alhambra for use at the
  Almansor Park baseball field. East Alhambra Little provided the funds for the scoreboard
  installation, and the City coordinated the work. Staff received three bids for the installation
  of the scoreboard. The lowest responsible bid was $11,000.00. East Alhambra Little
  League donated $11,000.00 to cover the costs of the scoreboard installation. After
  installation, the City would be responsible for ongoing maintenance of the scoreboard, but
  East Alhambra Little League would assume the responsibility for the remote-control
  system.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action:  City Council accepted from the East Alhambra Little League a donation of
  an electric outdoor baseball scoreboard at Almansor Park baseball field; accepted a cash
  donation of $11,000.00 for the installation of the scoreboard; directed the finance Director
  to appropriate the $11,000.00 in revenues and expenditures for the completion of the
  project; and, directed staff to undertake the steps necessary to finalize the Council’s
  action. (M2M26-58)

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded:  MAZA
  Ayes:  MAZA, LEE, WANG, ANDRADE-STADLER, MALONEY

   Staff requested that the City Council consider second reading and adoption of an
  ordinance approving an updated AB 481 Policy. On April 25, 2022, the City Council
  adopted Ordinance No. O2M22-4803 approving a Military Equipment Use Policy (“Policy”)
  pursuant to assembly Bill 481 (“AB 481”). In accordance with the legislation and the
  Policy, a military equipment report must be submitted to the City Council annually for each
  type of military equipment approved within one year of approval, and annually thereafter
  for as long as the military equipment is available for use. Alhambra’s 2025 Annual Military
  Equipment Report and the Police Department’s updated policy, are outlined in the Chief
  of Police’s staff report dated March 23, 2026. AB 481 requires that the Council determine,
  based on the annual military equipment report submitted pursuant to Section 7072,
  whether each type of military equipment identified in that report has complied with the
  standards for approval set forth in Government Code section 7071(d). Staff reviewed
  Department records and determined there were no complaints or concerns reported on
  the use of the equipment in 2025. Additionally, the Department conducted an internal audit
  and determined that there were no violations of the military equipment use policy. The
  proposed ordinance was given first reading at the March 23, 2026 City Council meeting.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council declared introduced for its second reading and adopted
  the following ordinance entitled:
  Ordinance No. O2M26-4858: An Ordinance of the City Council of the City of
  Alhambra implementing AB 481 by approving an updated policy for the use of
  military equipment by the Alhambra Police Department
